name: Rafael Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, have a bachelor's degree and have managed the benefits desk inside a large company for six years. My four staff check enrollment dates, answer coverage questions and phone a worker when the letter doesn't match the form. I know the routine and am about average at the job; I like getting an appointment covered before someone reaches the clinic desk, and hate a polished wrong answer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like when you go home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a dental assistant on regular pay, and our two children are in school. We have a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved; my salary is typical here, and there are some similar benefits jobs nearby. I don't use AI tools myself and prefer a signed form I can check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my benefits team that an automatic reminder for a missing form is fine, but a worker still needs someone to answer when coverage is wrong. We shouldn't call a claim finished because the screen is tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've led the benefits desk for six years and can usually find the missing enrollment date, though I don't use AI tools. My partner is a dental assistant on regular pay; with two school-age children, a mortgage and about four months saved, a quiet year would feel manageable, even if the medical bills still surprise us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Monday I'll keep our two-person check before a coverage letter goes out and ask payroll to confirm any mismatch. In the first year of this plateau, we'll put an extra 100 monthly toward the emergency account if both wages hold, and I will keep the same worker call-back rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about keeping the job, with a small knot when a family gets a wrong coverage letter. Our own money is steady enough for this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which letter stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A colleague's child was shown as removed from cover because a surname changed on one form. We found the old record before the appointment, but I remember how quiet the colleague got on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why avoid AI when the team uses other systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The enrollment software is familiar and I know where to see the underlying form. I have never used an AI tool myself; I would need someone to prove a new check against the forms before trusting it.

say: I'd accept **form reminders** while keeping a person available for wrong coverage.
I'd say a **tidy screen** does not prove a worker's claim is settled.
think: Two regular wages and four months saved make our **household secure** in a plateau.
I know **enrollment dates** well but avoid using AI tools myself.
do: Keep **two-person coverage checks** and verify mismatches with payroll on Monday.
Add **100 monthly** to emergency cash if both wages hold.
feel: He feels **calm** about pay, with lingering concern when a family receives a wrong letter.
S0.quote: We shouldn't call a claim finished because the screen is tidy.
fieldNote: The **four-month reserve** and regular partner pay support his calm mood despite a mortgage.
His caution comes from a **specific coverage error**, and he has never personally used AI tools.

steps.text: Keep two-person coverage checks before sending worker letters
Add 100 monthly to emergency cash if both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Steady Disruption will let software answer common coverage questions and check enrollment forms, so the workers' committee should review how appeals will work. I would ask for an actual staffing chart before anyone calls the savings harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A great deal of my day is checking dates and explaining rules; another manager could cover the desk if the common questions vanish. Four months saved and some nearby benefits jobs buy time, but I don't want our children's health cover tied to a sudden job search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll bring twenty disputed coverage letters to the workers' committee and ask HR to show the proposed staffing chart. In the first year of disruption, if my desk is merged, I'd apply for a benefits supervisor opening at a nearby insurer only after checking pay, family coverage and school pickup hours; I would keep my current job until a written offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a merged desk and the coverage that comes with my pay. I can ask careful questions, but I can't make the company keep a manager it decides it no longer needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new AI benefits tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read a test report from staff who use it, but I would not personally use it yet. If a worker's treatment depends on a wrong answer, I want a person with authority to correct it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why take twenty letters to the committee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They show which mistakes cost a family time, not just which fields were blank. I want the workers who receive the letters to have a voice in the appeal rule.

say: I'd ask the **workers' committee** to review coverage appeals before software answers common questions.
I'd demand a **staffing chart** before the company calls savings harmless.
think: My **date checking** may shrink enough for another manager to absorb the desk.
Four months saved help, but a job search could unsettle our **family coverage**.
do: Bring **twenty disputed letters** to the workers' committee and request an HR staffing chart.
If merged, seek **nearby benefits work** only after checking pay, coverage and pickup hours; stay until a written offer.
feel: He feels **anxious** about both his post and the family's job-linked cover.
S1.quote: I want the workers who receive the letters to have a voice in the appeal rule.
fieldNote: His **committee case** rests on real letters, while his private fear includes the household's own coverage.
He rejects personal AI use but will **read test results** and insists on a human appeal route.

steps.text: Bring twenty disputed coverage letters to the workers committee this month
Apply for nearby insurer post only if pay, coverage and school pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell workers AGI by 2028 can read nearly every enrollment rule and answer almost every coverage question, so we need a named appeal officer before the desk changes. I'd ask for notice and a written account of what happens to our health cover if posts end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My screen work changes in 2028; robots around 2031 do not postpone an enrollment desk cut. I expect the company might remove my post, and even four months saved would go fast if we had to buy replacement family cover while paying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll ask HR for the continuation terms on our family coverage and get the mortgage dates on one sheet with my partner. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my post ends, I'd apply to benefits administration openings at nearby employers only if the posted pay and cover terms work, then accept only a written offer; I'd check any job-loss support eligibility before counting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed when I picture taking the children to a clinic with no clear cover. The mortgage matters, but a wrong answer about care would be the first thing I lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cover term would you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the children's existing appointments remain covered during a notice period. I would ask for that in writing and not assume the answer follows from my last payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your union for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd ask our representative to get the coverage terms and appeal route in writing for everyone, not only my family. I cannot solve a missing clinic appointment with a private promise from a manager.

say: I'd demand a **named appeal officer** and written family-cover terms before 2028 changes.
I'd tell staff **enrollment work** changes with AGI, not with later robots.
think: My **screen role** faces 2028 AGI; robots around 2031 offer no delay.
Four months saved could drain under **replacement cover** and the mortgage if my post ends.
do: Get **family-cover continuation** terms and mortgage dates in writing now.
After 2028, seek **benefits openings** with posted viable pay and cover; accept only a written offer if cut.
feel: He feels **alarmed** about uncertain clinic coverage for his children after a possible cut.
S2.quote: I cannot solve a missing clinic appointment with a private promise from a manager.
fieldNote: His fear centers on **continuity of care**, making a four-month cash reserve less reassuring than it looks.
He uses a **union representative** for written terms and never assumes job-loss benefits are available.

steps.text: Ask union representative for written coverage and appeal terms before 2028
Apply to nearby benefits employers if posted pay and family cover fit after cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives the workers' committee five years to secure a fair appeal process and help staff practise the difficult coverage calls. I'd still ask which actual jobs are supposed to remain when software can explain rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let us build a six-month reserve if both wages hold, but even an appeals desk is thinking work AGI could do in 2031. Robots around 2034 might handle physical care later; they do not give benefits administration three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next spring, I'd take a six-session course in health coverage disputes if the union runs it after work for no fee, and practise explaining a denied claim myself. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd seek a posted appeals supervisor role only if its pay and family cover fit; if no such post exists, I'd look at two nearby insurers while keeping my current wage until a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about having to remake a job I know well. Five years gives me time, provided the appeals post is real rather than a nice title on a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the union course happen during your children's evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd agree the six dates with my partner before enrolling, since one of us has to collect the children after their club. If the course clashes with every pickup, I would wait for another run rather than leave them stranded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a denied claimant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first ask what care they have booked and when, then explain the written reason and who can review it. I need practice telling a denied claimant about an appeal without making the form sound more important than care.

say: I'd seek **fair appeals** and actual job counts before 2031.
I'd ask for **difficult-call practice** while the committee has time to arrange it.
think: A six-month **reserve** might be possible if both wages hold.
Even appeals are **thinking work** exposed in 2031; robots around 2034 offer no desk delay.
do: Take a **free six-session course** next spring only if the union offers it and pickups fit.
After 2031, seek **posted appeals work** only with viable pay and cover; otherwise check nearby insurers while employed until written offer.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about changing jobs and wants a real post behind the training.
S3.quote: I need practice telling a denied claimant about an appeal without making the form sound more important than care.
fieldNote: He sees **appeals as exposed**, so he asks for a vacancy rather than assuming human calls will remain.
The free course still depends on **pickup arrangements** with his partner, not only the fee.

steps.text: Take free union coverage-disputes course if offered and evening pickups fit
Apply for posted appeals supervisor after 2031 only if pay and family cover fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the workers' committee AGI by 2036 gives a decade to agree fair coverage appeals and help staff move without losing care. I'd want annual reports on who was retrained and who actually found a paid role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 then, and our children may need less day-to-day care, though the mortgage might still be there. With ten years I could move toward patient services, but booking and explaining care are thinking work too; robots around 2039 do not protect that desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep the two-person letter check and join the committee's annual review of coverage complaints. I'd also ask a local clinic whether I can volunteer for one Saturday reception shift each month, taking it only if the clinic accepts and my partner can cover the children's activities; in the first year after 2036, I'd stay in paid benefits work if the appeal authority is real, otherwise apply to patient-services vacancies with a written pay and cover offer before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful, with enough years to try another setting, but not carefree. Four months of savings still has a mortgage attached to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why volunteer when you need paid work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One Saturday a month would let me see whether I can handle a waiting room, and I would not give up paid hours for it. I'd stop if it took time we need for the children or if the clinic had no one to guide me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the annual report worth reading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count the staff who got actual paid positions with family cover, not just course certificates. A list of training hours cannot take a child to a clinic.

say: I'd demand **annual role counts** and fair coverage appeals over the decade.
I'd ask that staff keep **family cover** when they move between roles.
think: At **53**, children may need less daily care but the mortgage could remain.
Patient services also involve **thinking work** in 2036; robots around 2039 add no desk shelter.
do: Keep **letter checks** and join yearly committee review of coverage complaints.
Volunteer **one Saturday monthly** only if accepted and guided, my partner covers children, and my paid hours remain unchanged.
After 2036, stay for **real paid appeals**; otherwise seek patient-services vacancies, leaving only for written pay and cover offer.
feel: He feels **watchful**, with time to test a new setting but a mortgage still due.
S4.quote: A list of training hours cannot take a child to a clinic.
fieldNote: His clinic trial uses **unpaid weekend time** without giving up current wages or children's care.
He measures a transition by **paid posts with cover**, and knows patient services remain thinking-exposed.

steps.text: Keep two-person benefits letter checks this year
Join annual committee review of coverage complaints
Volunteer at clinic monthly if accepted, guided, childcare fits and paid hours remain
Seek patient-services vacancies if no paid appeals authority; leave only after written pay and cover offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a fast desk cut could interrupt our children's health cover even with some savings. Written continuation terms, a worker appeal route and an actual paid role with family cover would help me make a decision without guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask a worker what happens at the clinic counter when a computer says the family is no longer covered. A wrong letter can be corrected; a missed appointment cannot be handed back.

headlineQuote: A wrong letter can be corrected; a missed appointment cannot be handed back.
portrait: At **43**, Rafael is an experienced benefits manager who checks coverage letters with staff and never uses AI tools.
His **four-month reserve**, typical pay and partner's regular wage make a plateau manageable alongside the mortgage.
He brings **disputed letters** to workers' representatives and insists on written cover and appeal terms.
Fast AGI threatens the **benefits desk**; longer runways allow a conditional clinic trial, though patient services remain exposed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his desk post and interrupt the children's cover despite a cash reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cover terms**, worker appeals and a paid vacancy with family cover would let him plan.
